Another day, another sea of placards expected to spill out onto Europe’s streets.
Protests are set to continue on Saturday after tens of thousands filled the continent’s cities on Friday in a youth-led day of action across more than 25 nations.
Student groups in the UK, France, Spain, Italy and beyond walked out on Friday over the sky-rocketing cost of living, rising tuition fees, underfunded education systems and what they cast as leaders’ complicity in Israel’s war in Gaza. In Italy, trade unions also joined the protests and called on their members to observe a nationwide strike.
Other grievances that have prompted Gen-Z-led protests this fall include high unemployment, the climate crisis and fears governments are failing to future-proof against unregulated artificial intelligence.

“We don’t want to break off diplomatic relations with Russia in this particular situation that Denmark and Europe are in… But on the other hand, we want to send a very, very strong signal,” Rasmussen said.

Leaders from the United Kingdom and European Union have reached what’s been hailed as a “win-win” deal, in a summit held as British Prime Minister Andy Burnham pushes for a closer relationship with the bloc a decade after the Brexit vote.
A new package of agreements to create new opportunities for young people to live, study and travel on the continent, link emissions trading, and remove trade barriers on food products has been agreed, a UK government spokesperson told CNN on Friday.
Burnham welcomed the “landmark” deal, saying it draws a line “on a decade of drift and division by reconnecting with old friends.”
“We’re 10 years on from Brexit, but I think we can all confidently say this is a good day for Britain, and this is a good day for Europe. The agreement that we’ve reached together is a win-win,” he said at a news conference following the Brussels summit.
